1:
The outcry is sorted into classes before it is judged. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) explain that zealously as the rulers carried on the building, the work could not fail to burden the poorer classes, who found it hard to maintain their families and were still oppressed by wealthy usurers; and they distinguish three complaints: those with no property who wanted corn for their families, those obliged to mortgage fields and vineyards to buy it, and those who had mortgaged to pay the king’s tribute. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) marks what is new, that Nehemiah’s other troubles had come from the enemies without, and that he begins this account by laying emphasis on the hard treatment of Jews by Jews. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sums the causes in a phrase, that hard times and hard hearts made the poor miserable, and observes that the most necessitous families were the most numerous — here were the mouths, but where was the meat?

Whether there was a famine at all divides them. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reaches back to the judicial dearth of the prophet’s time, when the heaven was stayed from dew because the people ran each to his own house while the house of the Lord lay waste; but he thinks it more likely that a new dearth had come from the sheer number of people, for whose support the cultivated land was not sufficient. Henry takes the same chastisement and adds the withheld church dues, with the moral that foolish sinful men bring God’s judgments upon themselves and then fret and complain of them. Ellicott denies a famine outright: not any particular dearth, strictly speaking, but their present hunger, past mortgages having straitened their resources. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) offers three causes of his own: the multitude of people in and near Jerusalem, the work which took them up, and the expectation of invasion, which kept them from going abroad for provisions and the country people from bringing any in.

The tribute and the mortgages are read for their mechanics. Henry calls the king’s tribute a remaining mark of their captivity and guesses a poll-money, so that the more mouths a man had to maintain the more he paid — their families having come poor out of Babylon and been at great expense in building houses. Ellicott renders the clause literally, that they had made their fields and vineyards answerable for the payment of that tribute, having pledged the coming produce. Keil and Delitzsch correct the tense, since the participle shows the mortgaging had already taken place and was still in force: the sense is not that they must pledge their fields to procure corn, but that they have been obliged to pledge them and now ask for corn because of the dearth, what they could pledge being the crop or such part as equalled the sum borrowed.

The selling of the children is where all of them stop. Ellicott calls it the climax of the cry, the bondage of their children and especially the daughters, sold until the Jubile for money — children as precious to their parents as the rulers’ children to them. Wesley presses why the daughters are named, as evidence of necessity, since they were more tender and unfit for bond-service and more exposed to injuries than the sons, and notes that the redemption the law allowed was beyond their means. Henry gives the appeal its force: our children are as their children, as dear to us as theirs to them, free-born Israelites of the same holy nation, our flesh carrying the sacred seal of the covenant as well as our brethren’s. John Gill (reformed) puts the same claim plainly, that they are of one nature, nation, stock and religion with their creditors, their children circumcised as theirs and entitled to the same privileges in church and state.
6:
Nehemiah’s method is weighed against another reformer’s. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the comparison: Ezra and Nehemiah were both wise, good and useful men, yet in cases not unlike there was great difference in their management, for when Ezra was told of the rulers’ sin he rent his clothes and wept and was hardly persuaded to attempt a reformation, while Nehemiah forced them to reform. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) repeats the contrast in brief, adding that God’s work may be done and yet different methods taken in doing it, so that we should not arraign the management of others nor make our own the standard. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) credits the governor with self-command, since having recently arrived he had not known this state of things, and corrects the assembly’s description, which should read not against them but concerning them. John Gill (reformed) notes that the complaint raised both pity toward the poor and indignation at the rich.

What the nobles had done is harder to state than it looks. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls it expressly contrary to the law of God and doubly cruel at such a time, the people being just returned out of captivity and suffering from a dearth, reporting the view that this fell about a sabbatical year, when they were commanded to exact no debt. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) find the usual rendering unworkable, since the words mean simply to lend a loan and Nehemiah can hardly reproach the nobles for lending when he and his servants had done the same; the injustice must lie rather in the emphatic position given to the word for the pledge. Ellicott reaches the same difficulty from the other end, observing that the transgressors had violated the spirit rather than the letter of the law, so that the bare charge of exacting usury failed in its object. Gill notes the understatement in the words it is not good that ye do, by which much more is intended than is expressed.

The remedy is pressed from the governor’s own practice, then priced. Ellicott reads the appeal closely: he and his people have lent money and corn themselves, so he pleads by his own example not for leaving off usury but for remitting the loans outright. Wesley puts it plainly, that Nehemiah freely remits his own right and therefore they ought to do the same, since he lays no burden on them but what he will bear a part of himself. On the hundredth part Clarke relays a sharp challenge, that the word nowhere means a hundredth part, that neither the Syriac nor the Greek nor the Arabic acknowledges one, and that remitting a hundredth to people so distressed would have answered no end, so that it should rather be read as a part from the money; others take it for the monthly charge, which Ellicott and Wesley reckon at twelve per cent a year, now given up.

The oath and the gesture that sealed it close the business. Ellicott observes that a promise to restore the property and require no more interest had already been given, but that Nehemiah exacted an oath for legal validity, the priests’ presence lending the highest religious sanction; and he reads the shaking of the lap as imprecating on every covenant-breaker that he be emptied of all his possessions, as the fold of the garment was emptied. He adds that the iniquity thus stopped is not named in the later covenant, nor among the offences found on his second return. Clarke and Gill both set the gesture beside a Roman parallel, the ambassadors who entered the senate of Carthage with the toga gathered in the bosom, saying they carried peace and war, then shook out the fold and said, we bring you war. Wesley is content to call it a form of swearing then in use.
14:
The twelve years are first established. John Gill (reformed) reconstructs the appointment, that Nehemiah was made governor by the king of Persia not when first sent into Judea but probably after finishing the wall, the twentieth to the thirty-second year making twelve. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) infers from the same phrase: the narrative thus far was written after his return and on a review of his governorship, which is why nothing is said of the second appointment, then still in the future. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) qualifies the span, that he did not continue so long together at Jerusalem but governed it that long, by himself when present and by a deputy in his absence.

The predecessors are judged, the difference traced to one phrase. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) notes that Nehemiah does not name them, because what he had to say of them was not to their honour, and in such a case it is good to spare names; they suffered their servants to squeeze what they could out of the people. From which he draws two notes: that it is no new thing for men in public places to serve themselves by the public loss, and that masters must answer for the oppression they connive at in their servants. John Wesley repeats both points in brief. Ellicott prices the practice instead, taking the forty shekels as received over and above the bread and wine, some four pounds daily from the whole people, and judging that the governors meant cannot include Zerubbabel but only his successors. He then grounds the stated motive in the law itself, where usury and rigour are interdicted with the express sanction, fear thy God.

What he did instead of enriching himself is the burden of the passage. Henry insists on the purpose: he relates his practice not in pride or vain-glory but as an inducement to his successors and to the inferior magistrates to be tender of the people’s ease; and he presses the test of outcome, that the predecessors’ estates showed what a good hand they had made of their place, while Nehemiah got nothing but the satisfaction of doing good — say not then that he was a bad husband, but a good governor, who aimed not to feather his own nest. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) adds that neither he nor his officers took advantage of the people’s necessities to buy their lands, and that he even made his own servants work at the wall; with such an example it was scandalous for chiefs and priests to oppress an afflicted people. Ellicott renders the verb as repaired rather than continued, that is, as superintendent, and makes the same point, that instead of acquiring land by mortgage they were absorbed in the common work.

The table is described, and the chapter ends in prayer. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) identify the hundred and fifty as the heads of the houses of Judah, always his guests; the daily provision was one ox, six choice and therefore fat sheep, and fowls, at his own charge, with a quantity of wine every ten days which is not numbered but only called very great — and notwithstanding all this he did not require the allowance, because the service lay heavy upon the people. Clarke reckons it food for more than two hundred men, and compares a modern eastern ruler whose twelve sheep a day answered to six sheep and an ox, his nobles dining first, then the servants, then the poor. He supposes Nehemiah bore the cost out of money saved as cup-bearer at the Persian court. Ellicott corrects the last clause, which speaks not of bondage but of heavy service; and Gill reads the closing prayer as expecting no recompense from the people but from the Lord, and from him not in the way of merit but of grace.
